https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/14/fuel.text: Protests against fuel price increases spread across Syria for a second consecutive day on Monday, with demonstrators blocking roads and oil tanker routes in several provinces and calling for the dismissal of Energy Minister Mohammed al-Bashir, as parliament summoned him to appear before a hearing on Thursday.More than 50 members of Syria's People's Assembly signed a request on Sunday demanding the energy committee question al-Bashir over the price hikes and their impact on living conditions.The assembly confirmed on Monday that the hearing had been set for Thursday at noon local time (11 am CEST).Fuel prices rose by 25% to 40% after Syria's standing committee for the pricing of petroleum products issued a new temporary price list that took effect at midnight on Sunday.The price of a litre of 95-octane petrol rose from 152 to 195 new Syrian pounds, 90-octane from 147 to 185 pounds, and diesel from 125 to 175 pounds — an increase of 40%. A household gas cylinder rose from 1,470 to 1,600 pounds.100 Syrian pounds is about 1 eurocent, but the average net monthly salary in Syria varies widely by sector and can amount to just €50 to €60, according to publicly available figures.The government of interim President Ahmed al-Sharaa has increased the minimum wage by 550% in March, as part of a broader recovery plan for the Middle Eastern country whose years-long civil war devastated most of its economy and resulted in the deaths of more than 580,000 people, with another 13.5 million displaced.Protests were reported in Hasakah, Deir ez-Zor, Raqqa, Aleppo, Idlib and Daraa. In Hasakah and Deir ez-Zor, demonstrators blocked roads used by crude oil tankers and cut the al-Suway'iya bridge crossing between Syria and Iraq near al-Bukamal.In the city of al-Shahil, residents blocked the road leading to the al-Omar oilfield, preventing tankers from passing.In Raqqa, truck and haulage drivers staged a sit-in outside a grain storage centre, with the road to the silos remaining blocked on Monday.In Idlib province, protesters blocked the M5 motorway near Maaret al-Numan, while video circulating online showed a night-time demonstration in the city of Idlib with crowds demanding al-Bashir's removal.Local sources reported that a young man in Hasakah province attempted to set himself on fire in protest at the price increases and worsening living conditions before bystanders intervened. Video of a separate incident showed another man threatening to burn his car. Euronews could not independently confirm these reports.Al-Bashir said on Saturday the price rise was needed to bridge a gap between the cost of importing petroleum products and their domestic selling prices.Syria produces approximately 102,000 barrels of oil per day against domestic demand of around 325,000 barrels, leaving it heavily dependent on imports, he said.Major maintenance work at the Baniyas refinery in the southern Tartus governorate has further reduced domestic refining capacity, requiring additional imports of finished petroleum products.The ministry said it would review prices as global market conditions change and the refinery returns to full capacity. Oil prices have risen above $100 a barrel in recent days amid disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz linked to the Iran war and Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.

Photograph: Jonas Ekstromer/EPA This Is Europe Sweden Sweden voted against more power for the far right – but are centrists listening? Even as the ‘extremist’ AfD seeks further election gains in Germany, Europe’s leaders can learn from Sweden’s dangerous embrace with far-right ideology Don’t get This Is Europe delivered to your inbox? Sign up here Katherine Butler , associate editor, Europe Wed 16 Sep 2026 11.45 EDT Last modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 11.46 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google E urope’s focus turned nervously to Sweden on Sunday, after an explosive election in Germany just a week earlier placed a far-right party, officially classed as “extremist”, on the brink of power in a German state for the first time since the Nazi era. A party with neo-Nazi roots has been pulling the government’s strings in Sweden for the last four years – would the country’s general election put the far right formally in government? Or would enough Swedes opt for a gear change, having seen the Sweden Democrats’ hardline (some would say poisonous ) agenda in action? Votes were still being counted on Wednesday but it was immediately clear that the far-right Sweden Democrats had suffered a setback ; their first loss of support among voters since it entered parliament for the first time 16 years ago. The party slipped from being the country’s second biggest party to its third. The centre-left Social Democrats appear poised for a return to power, although it could take months for their leader, Magdalena Andersson, to form a coalition. Strong results for the left and green parties gave her left bloc a wafer-thin, three-seat majority. Is the far right’s regression, however modest, a turning point? Have Swedes reached the limits of a taboo-busting experiment with populist, nationalist rightwing prescriptions? And is there a message for mainstream leaders across Europe , many of whom seem fatalistic about a continental far-right surge? France goes to the polls in April while governments in Italy, Spain and Poland, all face their electorates later next year. The Dutch political scientist Cas Mudde says elections in one country are a poor guide to what will happen in another. Specific local factors in Sweden, including a scandal, may have dented the far right’s support. For Mudde, the scale of the AfD’s win in Saxony Anhalt, however, was “ a black day for Europe ” – and with far-right ideas gaining ground across the continent, he warned mainstream politicians that “today’s key fight is for democracy, rather than for party or power”. This is where Sweden offers a cautionary tale. Its political establishment had “fully normalised” the far-right party, Mudde said. “Its nativism is now shared by all the major parties, albeit in lighter form, from the Moderates on the right to the Social Democrats on the left.” But the decline in the far right’s support, for now, he thinks, “at the very least creates space for mainstream parties to focus on issues other than immigration”. Ann-Cathrine Jungar, a professor of political science at Södertörn University in Stockholm, is very sure that the Sweden Democrats are not on the way out. Electoral rankings go up and down, she said, and the party’s influence will endure. More important now is how the mainstream parties respond. “We focus a lot on the extreme and radical right parties, but the key to their influence is what the other parties do. Why have Sweden’s mainstream parties adopted the far right’s policies? The Social Democrats have co-opted their ideas, even though they are counter to the country’s needs. In Sweden, we need competent, talented people who want to come and live here, we need labour for health and social care. Yet nationalism seems to be the prevailing ideology now.” In a widely read Guardian essay headlined How Sweden lost its soul – and stopped being Sweden, published before the vote, Martin Gelin documented his country’s transformation after 2022. Rightwing parties that year signed a Faustian pact with the Sweden Democrats, buying its support for a minority rightwing government. The deal? The far right was given a direct hand in shaping policy. “A new Sweden has emerged, cruel and cold for migrants”, wrote Gelin, with xenophobic and ethno-nationalist ideas “now comfortably embedded in the political mainstream”. Most shockingly, Andersson’s Social Democrats, modelling themselves on their hardline Danish counterparts, had bought into the far right’s framings on crime and immigration. Will Sweden’s Social Democrats now learn from their worst performance in more than 100 years, and embrace an agenda that does not involve deporting toddlers to Iran, people with dementia to the UK , or locking up 14-year-olds? Jungar is sceptical. “When it comes to linking crime and immigration, this is the new normal,” she said. “The Social Democrats will not pursue policies that are more liberal.” Yet the political centre in Sweden could articulate a clear alternative to the far right, Mudde says. The Left and the Greens did significantly better among young voters in this week’s election. “This reflects a development we see across Europe , namely that young people prefer outspokenly leftwing parties over centre-left parties.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion Ghosts of grievance View image in fullscreen Ulrich Siegmund (centre), head of the AfD state parliamentary group in Saxony-Anhalt, celebrates his party’s election win with parliamentary leaders Alice Weidel (left) and Tino Chrupalla (right). Photograph: Michael Kappeler/DPA/AP Like Giorgia Meloni’s party, Brothers of Italy, and Marine Le Pen’s National Rally in France, the Sweden Democrats have “deradicalised” in selective ways, to broaden their appeal, Jungar told me. By contrast, what was striking in Germany, was how the AfD doubled its score to 44% of the vote, on what Constanze Stelzenmuller in the FT called “ a programme of stunning malevolence” . Two further regional elections this Sunday in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania will be closely watched, including by the AfD’s American backers such as Elon Musk . Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania has economic and demographic conditions comparable to Saxony Anhalt. For those struggling to understand the appeal of the AfD in eastern Germany, Carolin Würfel’s essay offered an original insight . Born in the former East Germany, Würfel believes that many voters there don’t actually know or care about the AfD’s detailed policies. But the party had tapped into a legacy of grievance about the economic impact of reunification in the 1990s. “Villages and small towns that had been hollowed out, some of them ghostly and depopulated, were suddenly told again: you matter. Everyone else may have left you behind, but I, we, the AfD, care.” The AfD won’t improve life in east Germany, Würfel wrote, “but that was never the point”. As in Sweden, the political centre in Germany is now being warned that time is running out to offer a credible democratic alternative to the far right. As Florian Ranft of the Das Progressive Zentrum thinktank wrote : “Waiting for the AfD to fail is not a strategy.” To receive the complete version of This Is Europe in your inbox every Wednesday, please subscribe here . Photograph: Patrick T Fallon/Bloomberg via Getty Images View image in fullscreen Phil Knight, chair and cofounder of Nike Inc, arrives for a session at the Allen & Co Media and Technology Conference in Sun Valley, Idaho, on 11 July 2019. Photograph: Patrick T Fallon/Bloomberg via Getty Images Oregon Nike cofounder gives $1bn to University of Oregon in historic donation Phil Knight and wife, Penny, make largest known donation to a public university to fund a new engineering school Anna Betts Wed 23 Sep 2026 11.13 EDT First published on Wed 23 Sep 2026 10.40 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Nike cofounder Phil Knight, and his wife, Penny, have donated $1bn to the University of Oregon in what the university described as the “largest gift ever made to a comprehensive public university”. The donation is intended to be used to establish a new engineering school in Eugene. In a news release, seen by the Guardian, the university said the new school “will educate engineers and applied scientists in bioengineering and other high-demand disciplines, attract faculty and researchers to a growing campus, and accelerate the university’s ability to move discoveries out of the laboratory and into products, therapies, technologies and companies”. The University of Oregon’s president, Karl Scholz, said in a statement Wednesday morning that the Knights have “a long history of believing in things before they exist” and that “they did it in 2016, and they are doing it again now, at a scale that is genuinely hard to take in. I am grateful to them, and I am grateful to be here for it.” Knight, 88, is a graduate of the university. The latest donation brings the Knight family’s known total giving to the University of Oregon to more than $2bn, according to the New York Times . The school said in the news release on Wednesday that the gift is the third commitment the Knights have made at this scale in 10 years, following $500m in 2016 and $500m in 2021 that created and expanded the Knight Campus. The school also said the new engineering school will be located at the Phil and Penny Knight Campus for Accelerating Scientific Impact. In the announcement, Knight also shared a statement noting that “to make an audacious dream a reality requires more than a vivid imagination”. “It also requires the sort of opportunity that our great American universities, both public and private, have historically provided,” he said. “This is no time to abandon them.” He added: “Penny and I are grateful for the chance to invest in our most promising young people’s future in this important way.” Bob Guldberg, vice-president and Robert and Leona DeArmond executive director of the Knight Campus, said in a statement that the creation of a college of engineering “builds on the original vision put forward by UO faculty who inspired Phil and Penny to invest in the idea that we can do better translating the great work we do out into the real world”. “The Knight Campus stands on the foundation of a remarkable Oregon legacy: the belief that bold innovation can unlock human potential,” Guldberg said. “Today, we carry that same belief forward, applying it to science, technology, and human health.” Scholz, the university president, said in an interview with the New York Times about the donation that “one of the most successful businesspeople in the history of humanity, and one of the most generous philanthropists in the history of humanity, has said higher education is worth an investment of this magnitude. “At a time when we’re all feeling a little bit under siege, this is tremendous news,” he said, adding that the gift amounted to “a screaming endorsement of the importance of what we’re doing”. Senator Ron Wyden, an Oregon Democrat, said in a statement that “this groundbreaking gift from Phil and Penny Knight stands out for its extraordinary generosity and monumental impact at a public university”. “As a proud University of Oregon alumnus, I know my alma mater will put this massive investment to great use by educating students who will meet the ongoing need for engineers so essential to the economy in our state and nationwide,” he added. The news on Wednesday comes as earlier this month it was announced that the Knights were committing $1.1bn to Providence St Vincent Medical Center and to Providence Heart Institute to create Oregon’s first hospital dedicated exclusively to women’s health. “Penny and I have always believed that real breakthroughs come from people willing to take on the toughest challenges,” Knight said in a statement earlier this month. “Providence has shown that kind of ambition in cardiovascular care, and we see the same opportunity to do something truly distinctive for women’s health. We’re proud to invest in teams that will change what’s possible for communities across Oregon and beyond.” Last year, Oregon Health & Science University announced that it had received a $2bn commitment from the Knights to its cancer institute, which the university said would “transform the future of cancer care and set a new standard globally”. Pete Hegseth: ‘We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it.’ Photograph: Eric Lee/Reuters View image in fullscreen Pete Hegseth: ‘We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it.’ Photograph: Eric Lee/Reuters First Thing newsletter US news First Thing: Hegseth promises execution live stream as Trump appears to ‘pause’ war on Iran US president says US will not attack Iran before midterms, while defense secretary says Nidal Hasan will face a firing squad next month. Plus, Sofia Coppola looks back on her glittering directorial career Martin Belam Fri 9 Oct 2026 06.49 EDT Last modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 07.05 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Good morning. The defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, has said the execution of Nidal Hasan by firing squad will be livestreamed next month, in a radical departure from the previous norm. Hegseth said: “We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand there’s serious consequences for these types of things.” Hasan opened fire at a medical processing center at Fort Hood, Texas, on 5 November 2009, killing 13 people and wounding dozens more. A military jury sentenced him to death in 2013 and he has been held at Fort Leavenworth in Kansas ever since. The last known case of a military firing squad in the US was in November 1945. Why is Hegseth being criticised over the Iran war? The Democratic senator Chris Murphy said Hegseth was “determined to hide the cost and the consequences of this war from the American public”. Murphy claimed the Pentagon blocked him from visiting a military base in Qatar and that an Iranian strike on the US embassy in Riyadh was far worse than the public were led to believe. What has Donald Trump said about the US war on Iran? The US president has promised not to attack Iran before November’s US midterm elections , outlining a pause on the protracted war he has struggled to end after almost eight months. A Reuters/Ipsos survey from late September found that only about a third of Americans approved of the strikes on Iran. Billionaires fund California ballot measure to make voters show ID at polls View image in fullscreen Voters in Orange County, California. Photograph: MediaNews Group/Orange County Register/Getty Images Billionaires across the US are spending vast sums to support California’s Proposition 39, a measure that would require voters to show identification before casting their ballots. The measure is being promoted amid a nationwide push by the Trump administration to restrict voting. California Republicans have long sought to advance a voter ID initiative in the state. Various out-of-state conservative donors have given millions of dollars in support . Why are some voters calling Missouri’s elections ‘dizzying and embarrassing’? Thanks to a protracted legal battle over an effort by Republicans to redraw the state’s congressional map, some voters are no longer sure which congressional district they live in or who will be on their ballot paper for the midterms. What happened in last night’s crucial midterm debates? Rachel Leingang, George Chidi and Auzzy Byrdsell have rounded up the key takeaways from debates in the battleground states of Michigan, Georgia and Maine. Trump made clear that media ban was due to critical coverage, court told View image in fullscreen The CNN booth at the White House. Photograph: Evan Vucci/Reuters A lawyer who has represented numerous media companies that have sued the Trump administration over access issues has told a court that Donald Trump’s own words are one of the strongest parts of their case , after the US president made clear in a recent interview with Time magazine that he chose to bar three news organizations because of their critical coverage of him. CNN, MS Now and Politico were asking the judge to extend the temporary restraining order he issued on 24 September requiring the White House to lift the ban for 14 days. The district court judge Timothy Kelly – a Trump appointee – said he would extend it until next Tuesday. That means the White House will be forced to allow journalists from CNN, MS Now and Politico to continue accessing the building until then. Film shoot appearing to echo Renee Good killing roils Montana town View image in fullscreen Flowers and photos are left at a memorial site for Renee Good. Photograph: Alex Brandon/AP A Daily Wire film production that appears to re-enact elements of Renee Good’s killing has been allowed to continue filming in a rural Montana town. The project, which reportedly stars Danny Trejo and Harvey Keitel, follows an ICE agent’s effort to escape a mob seeking to free an immigrant he has detained, according to its logline. In one video of the shoot that surfaced online, a female actor portraying a protester can be seen driving a beat-up car into a flock of law enforcement agents, knocking one officer down as another fires his weapon. Then, the car abruptly lurches back. That scene drew backlash – and real protesters – over its resemblance to an ICE agent’s fatal shooting of Good in January. In other news … View image in fullscreen SpaceX Crew-12 members. Photograph: Anil Menon/Nasa/AP Four astronauts have returned to Earth from the International Space Station after a medical relief mission. The crew hurried to the ISS eight months ago after an astronaut fell ill in space. The DoJ is seeking to charge the ex-Trump aide Cassidy Hutchinson , who gave key testimony on the January 6 attack on the Capitol. She said she had been told that Trump lunged for the wheel of an SUV to try to join the mob. An ICE agent shot and injured a man in New York City during an enforcement operation, federal officials said. Trump says he is considering asking the FBI to investigate the death of Nolan Wells. Wells’s cause and manner of death are still undetermined, and a Jackson County grand jury declined to indict anyone in his case. Stat of the day: Thousands turn out to welcome weary USS Lincoln sailors after grueling deployment View image in fullscreen The USS Abraham Lincoln returns. Photograph: Mike Blake/Reuters Thousands of people flooded to greet the USS Lincoln’s long-awaited return . It left San Diego last November, expected to return in the spring, until the US and Israel launched the war with Iran. Culture pick: As pointless as a film based on a toy car could be … View image in fullscreen A still from Matchbox the movie. Photograph: Apple TV Enjoy a review that gives something an absolute battering? I can recommend Benjamin Lee on Matchbox , who says “John Cena and Jessica Biel collect paychecks in a soulless and synthetic slab of corporate product”. Elsewhere, Rich Pelley speaks to someone who has been behind films with a lot more soul. Sofia Coppola is, as you’d expect, a compelling read . Don’t miss this: ‘Delights await!’ – Margaret Atwood and other writers on Nobel winner Anne Carson View image in fullscreen Anne Carson. Photograph: Pontus Lundahl/TT News Agency/AP The Handmaid’s Tale author is joined by Emily Wilson, Ocean Vuong and the Booker-shortlisted writer Rebecca Perry in celebrating the newly announced Nobel laureate . … or this: How a plant selfie in Colombian jungle led to ‘jaw dropping’ giant waterlily find View image in fullscreen Jeremiah Harris in one of the pictures he posted on Instagram that was seen by a waterlily expert. Photograph: Jeremiah Harris The species, with leaves large enough to be seen from space, is already considered critically endangered – but plans are afoot to protect it . Climate check: Millions on alert as Hurricane Isaias set to bring dangerous storm surge View image in fullscreen Storm preparations in Alabama. Photograph: Octavio Jones/AP Millions of people from Louisiana to Florida were under hurricane warnings as Hurricane Isaias heads toward the US Gulf coast, with weather officials warning of hurricane-force winds, heavy rainfall and flooding. Storm surge warnings are already in effect from the mouth of the Mississippi River to the Suwanee River in Florida. When it makes its expected landfall, experts say it will be the biggest test for Fema since the Trump-imposed cuts on the agency. Last Thing: Astronomers detect mysterious burst of energy from a galaxy far, far away View image in fullscreen The MeerKat radio telescope. Photograph: Brendon Wainwright/Wikipedia I love a space mystery, and scientists have detected a fast radio burst that traveled for more than 10bn years before reaching Earth. The burst is believed to be the farthest yet detected, more than double the previous distance record. And nobody knows what they are.
